title: Decision Trees III - Regression Trees
abstract:
The same recursive algorithm, with one substitution: entropy and Gini are replaced
by variance, and the leaf outputs a mean rather than a majority. This document
derives why the mean is the optimal leaf value under squared error, works the
split search by variance reduction, explains the step-function output and its
consequences — most importantly that a tree cannot extrapolate — and covers
the hyperparameters and the alternative criteria (MAE, Poisson, Friedman-MSE)
that appear in scikit-learn.

blocks.t: What Changes
From the notes
Regression — focus on error minimization.

items:
Splitting criteria: 1. Try splitting on each feature.
 2. Calculate error after each split. 3. Choose the split with min error.
 4. Repeat for child nodes.

blocks.t: The Impurity Measure
Variance as impurity
For a node $S$ containing targets $y_i$:

\boxed{ I(S)=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{i\in S}\left(y_i-\bar y_S\right)^{2} }
 \qquad \bar y_S=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{i\in S}y_i

This is the variance of the node, and also the MSE of predicting $\bar y_S$ for
every member. It plays exactly the role entropy plays in classification: zero
when the node is "pure" (all targets equal), and large when they are spread out.
Why the mean is the optimal leaf value

Suppose a leaf must predict a single constant $c$ for all its members. Minimising
the squared error,

\frac{\partial}{\partial c}\sum_{i\in S}\left(y_i-c\right)^{2}
 = -2\sum_{i\in S}\left(y_i-c\right)=0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 c=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{i\in S}y_i=\bar y_S .

So the mean is not a convention — it is the minimiser, and the residual
error at that optimum is exactly the node's variance. Impurity measure and leaf
value come from the same calculation.

If instead you minimise absolute error, the optimum is the median,
which is what criterion="absolute_error" uses.
The Split Search
Variance reduction
Exactly the classification formula with $I$ replaced:
\Delta = I(S)-\left[\frac{|S_L|}{|S|}I(S_L)+\frac{|S_R|}{|S|}I(S_R)\right]

Try every feature and every candidate threshold; take the split maximising
$\Delta$ — equivalently, minimising the weighted child variance. This is the
notes' "try splitting on each feature, calculate error after each split,
choose the split with min error".

blocks.cap:
Left: the weighted child variance for every candidate threshold. The
 minimum is the chosen split, and it sits well below the parent's variance —
 that difference is the variance reduction. Right: the resulting depth-1 tree,
 with each leaf predicting the mean of its rows.

blocks.t: The computation is cheap

Sorting each feature once lets you sweep the threshold and update the child means
and variances incrementally, so one node costs $O(np\log n)$ rather than
$O(n^2p)$. This is why trees are fast to fit despite considering every possible
split.
The Output Is a Step Function

blocks.cap:
Increasing depth produces more, narrower steps. The tree never draws a
 smooth curve — it approximates one with a staircase, and an unconstrained tree
 ends with one step per training point.

blocks.t: Three consequences of piecewise-constant output

items:
A smooth trend needs many splits. A straight line
 $y=2x$ — which linear regression captures with one parameter — requires
 a deep tree to approximate, and the approximation is still a staircase.

It cannot extrapolate. Every prediction is a mean of observed
 targets, so the output is bounded by $[\min y,\max y]$ and is flat outside
 the training range.

Predictions are discrete. A tree with $L$ leaves can output at
 most $L$ distinct values, however many rows you score.

blocks.cap:
Left: outside the training range the tree returns a constant while a
 linear model continues the trend. Right: training MSE falls to zero with depth
 while test MSE is U-shaped — the bias–variance tradeoff of Topic 40, in a
 tree.

blocks.t: The extrapolation failure is silent

A tree asked to price a house twice the size of anything it has seen returns the
mean of its largest leaf, confidently and without warning. For time series with a
trend this is fatal: a tree forecasting sales will simply repeat the last level it
learned. The standard remedies are to model the trend separately (fit a tree to
the detrended residuals), or to use a linear model where extrapolation is
required.
Criteria and Hyperparameters

head: criterion
Leaf value
Use when
rows: Outliers in the target; far slower to fit
Inside gradient boosting — a variant of MSE with a better split score for boosted trees
The blunt, effective control on complexity
Especially important for regression — a leaf with 1–2 rows predicts a single noisy observation
Minimum rows required to attempt a split
Grows best-first rather than depth-first; often better than max_depth
Refuse splits that reduce variance by less than a threshold

blocks.t: min_samples_leaf matters more here than in classification

A classification leaf with three rows still outputs a majority vote, which is at
least a bounded guess. A regression leaf with one row outputs that row's
target — pure noise. Setting min_samples_leaf to 5–20 is one of the
cheapest and most effective regularisers for a regression tree.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor, export_text
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 300
x = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 10, n))
y = np.sin(x * .8) * 3 + x * .4 + rng.normal(0, .7, n)
X = x.reshape(-1, 1)

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE MEAN IS THE OPTIMAL LEAF VALUE -- verified
# =====================================================================
leaf = y[:40]
grid = np.linspace(leaf.min(), leaf.max(), 4000)
mse_at = [np.mean((leaf - c) ** 2) for c in grid]
mae_at = [np.mean(np.abs(leaf - c)) for c in grid]
print(f"MSE-optimal constant {grid[np.argmin(mse_at)]:.4f}   mean   {leaf.mean():.4f}")
print(f"MAE-optimal constant {grid[np.argmin(mae_at)]:.4f}   median {np.median(leaf):.4f}")
# The impurity measure and the leaf value come from the SAME calculation.

print(f"\nresidual error at the mean = {np.mean((leaf-leaf.mean())**2):.4f}")
print(f"variance of the leaf       = {leaf.var():.4f}   <- identical")

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE SPLIT SEARCH BY VARIANCE REDUCTION
# =====================================================================
def weighted_variance(x, y, c):
    L = x <= c
    if L.sum() < 2 or (~L).sum() < 2:
        return np.inf
    return L.mean() * y[L].var() + (~L).mean() * y[~L].var()

parent = y.var()
cands = (np.unique(x)[:-1] + np.unique(x)[1:]) / 2      # midpoints
costs = np.array([weighted_variance(x, y, c) for c in cands])
best = cands[np.argmin(costs)]

print(f"\nparent variance          {parent:.4f}")
print(f"best weighted child var  {costs.min():.4f}")
print(f"variance reduction       {parent - costs.min():.4f}")
print(f"scratch best threshold   {best:.4f}")

sk = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=1, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
print(f"sklearn root threshold   {sk.tree_.threshold[0]:.4f}")
print(f"sklearn root impurity    {sk.tree_.impurity[0]:.4f}  (== parent variance)")

# The two leaf values ARE the two group means:
L = x <= sk.tree_.threshold[0]
print(f"\nleaf means: {y[L].mean():.4f}  {y[~L].mean():.4f}")
print(f"sklearn    : {sk.tree_.value.ravel()[1]:.4f}  {sk.tree_.value.ravel()[2]:.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. A REGRESSION TREE FROM SCRATCH
# =====================================================================
def build(x, y, depth, max_depth, min_leaf=5):
    if depth >= max_depth or len(y) < 2 * min_leaf or y.var() < 1e-12:
        return {"leaf": float(y.mean()), "n": len(y)}
    cands = (np.unique(x)[:-1] + np.unique(x)[1:]) / 2
    best_c, best_cost = None, np.inf
    for c in cands:
        L = x <= c
        if L.sum() < min_leaf or (~L).sum() < min_leaf:
            continue
        cost = L.mean() * y[L].var() + (~L).mean() * y[~L].var()
        if cost < best_cost:
            best_c, best_cost = c, cost
    if best_c is None:
        return {"leaf": float(y.mean()), "n": len(y)}
    L = x <= best_c
    return {"thr": float(best_c),
            "left":  build(x[L],  y[L],  depth+1, max_depth, min_leaf),
            "right": build(x[~L], y[~L], depth+1, max_depth, min_leaf)}

def predict_one(node, v):
    while "leaf" not in node:
        node = node["left"] if v <= node["thr"] else node["right"]
    return node["leaf"]

tree = build(x, y, 0, max_depth=3)
scratch = np.array([predict_one(tree, v) for v in x])
skl = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=5,
                            random_state=0).fit(X, y).predict(X)
print(f"\nscratch MSE {np.mean((y-scratch)**2):.5f}   "
      f"sklearn MSE {np.mean((y-skl)**2):.5f}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. THE OUTPUT IS A STEP FUNCTION
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'max_depth':>10s} {'leaves':>8s} {'distinct predictions':>22s}")
for d in [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, None]:
    m = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=d, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
    print(f"{str(d):>10s} {m.get_n_leaves():8d} "
          f"{len(np.unique(m.predict(X))):22d}")
# A tree with L leaves can emit at most L distinct values, ever.

# =====================================================================
# 5. IT CANNOT EXTRAPOLATE
# =====================================================================
tree_m = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=5, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
lin_m  = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
far = np.array([[12.], [20.], [50.], [1000.]])
print(f"\n{'x':>8s} {'tree':>10s} {'linear':>10s}")
for v, t_, l_ in zip(far.ravel(), tree_m.predict(far), lin_m.predict(far)):
    print(f"{v:8.0f} {t_:10.3f} {l_:10.3f}")
print(f"training target range: [{y.min():.3f}, {y.max():.3f}]")
print(f"tree predictions are bounded by it: "
      f"{y.min() <= tree_m.predict(far).min() and tree_m.predict(far).max() <= y.max()}")

# A LINEAR TREND is the worst case for a tree:
xt = np.linspace(0, 20, 400)
yt = 2 * xt + rng.normal(0, 1, 400)
xtr, xte = xt[:250], xt[250:]                    # train on the FIRST part only
ytr, yte = yt[:250], yt[250:]
print(f"\nlinear trend, extrapolating:")
print(f"  tree   test MSE {mean_squared_error(yte, DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=6).fit(xtr[:,None], ytr).predict(xte[:,None])):.2f}")
print(f"  linear test MSE {mean_squared_error(yte, LinearRegression().fit(xtr[:,None], ytr).predict(xte[:,None])):.2f}")
# The tree is catastrophically worse -- it repeats its last learned level.

# =====================================================================
# 6. IT OVERFITS -- and min_samples_leaf is the key regulariser
# =====================================================================
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3, random_state=0)
print(f"\n{'max_depth':>10s} {'train MSE':>11s} {'test MSE':>10s} {'leaves':>8s}")
for d in [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, None]:
    m = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=d, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{str(d):>10s} {mean_squared_error(y_tr, m.predict(X_tr)):11.5f} "
          f"{mean_squared_error(y_te, m.predict(X_te)):10.5f} {m.get_n_leaves():8d}")
# Unconstrained: training MSE is 0.000 -- one leaf per row, predicting that
# row's own noisy target.

print(f"\n{'min_samples_leaf':>17s} {'test MSE':>10s} {'leaves':>8s}")
for ml in [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50]:
    m = DecisionTreeRegressor(min_samples_leaf=ml, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{ml:17d} {mean_squared_error(y_te, m.predict(X_te)):10.5f} "
          f"{m.get_n_leaves():8d}")
# min_samples_leaf=1 lets a leaf predict a single noisy observation.

# =====================================================================
# 7. THE CRITERIA
# =====================================================================
y_out = y.copy(); y_out[:8] += 40                # a few corrupted targets
print(f"\n{'criterion':>18s} {'test MSE':>10s} {'test MAE':>10s}")
for crit in ["squared_error", "absolute_error", "friedman_mse"]:
    m = DecisionTreeRegressor(criterion=crit, max_depth=4,
                              random_state=0).fit(X[:200], y_out[:200])
    p = m.predict(X[200:])
    print(f"{crit:>18s} {np.mean((y[200:]-p)**2):10.4f} "
          f"{np.mean(np.abs(y[200:]-p)):10.4f}")
# absolute_error uses the MEDIAN in each leaf, so it resists the corrupted
# targets -- at the cost of being much slower to fit.

# =====================================================================
# 8. TUNING
# =====================================================================
gs = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0),
                  {"max_depth": [2, 3, 4, 6, 8, None],
                   "min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 10, 20],
                   "max_leaf_nodes": [None, 8, 16, 32]},
                  cv=5, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error", n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"\nbest: {gs.best_params_}")
print(f"cv MSE {-gs.best_score_:.5f}   test MSE "
      f"{mean_squared_error(y_te, gs.predict(X_te)):.5f}")

print("\n", export_text(DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(X, y),
                        feature_names=["x"], decimals=3))
# Each leaf line shows 'value: ...' -- that number is the MEAN of its rows.
Worked Examples
A regression tree split by variance reduction
Data $x = [1,2,3,4,5,6]$, $y = [1,2,3,8,9,10]$. A regression tree picks the split that most reduces the sum of squared errors (SSE). The root prediction is the mean $\bar y = 5.5$.
Step 1 – root SSE. $\sum (y_i - 5.5)^2 = 77.5$.
Step 2 – try each threshold. Splitting at $x \le s$ and predicting each side's mean:
Step 3 – the winning split. $s = 3.5$ reduces SSE from $77.5$ to $4.0$. Left leaf: $\{1,2,3\}$, prediction $2$. Right leaf: $\{8,9,10\}$, prediction $9$.

Key idea. The tree's prediction is a constant inside each leaf, so the whole fit is a step function. More splits give more steps. This is why a single deep tree overfits, and why ensembles of trees are used.
Summary
Everything on one page

Regression trees focus on error minimization; the target
 value is numerical.

Splitting criteria: try splitting on each feature $\to$ calculate
 the error after each split $\to$ choose the split with minimum error
 $\to$ repeat for child nodes.

The impurity is the node's variance
 $I(S)=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum(y_i-\bar y_S)^2$, and the split score is
 variance reduction — the exact analogue of information gain.

The leaf predicts the mean, and that is not a convention: the
 mean is the minimiser of squared error, and the residual at that optimum
 is the variance. With absolute error the optimum is the median.

The output is a step function: a tree with $L$ leaves can emit at

It cannot extrapolate. Predictions are bounded by the observed
 target range and flat outside the training range — which makes trees a

A smooth trend needs many splits; an unconstrained tree reaches zero

 (median, outlier-robust, slow), friedman_mse (used inside
 gradient boosting), poisson (counts).

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. How does a regression tree differ from a classification tree?

Only in the impurity measure and the leaf output. Variance replaces entropy or
Gini, and the leaf predicts the mean rather than the majority class. The greedy
recursion, the stopping rules and the pruning are identical.
Q. Why does a leaf predict the mean?

Because the mean minimises squared error. Differentiating
$\sum(y_i-c)^2$ with respect to $c$ and setting it to zero gives
$c=\bar y$ — and the residual error at that optimum is exactly the node's
variance, which is why the impurity measure and the leaf value come from the same
calculation.
Q. Can a regression tree extrapolate?

No. Every prediction is the mean of some set of observed targets, so the output
is bounded by the training target range and is constant outside the training
range. A tree forecasting a trending time series simply repeats its last learned
level.
Q. Why is the output a step function?

Because the tree partitions the feature space into boxes and predicts one constant
per box. It cannot produce a smooth curve — only a staircase, with the number of
steps bounded by the number of leaves.
Q. Which hyperparameter matters most for a regression tree?

min_samples_leaf. With the default of 1, a leaf can contain a single row
and predict that row's own noisy target — pure memorisation. Setting it to 5–20
is one of the cheapest effective regularisers, and it matters more here than in
classification, where a small leaf at least outputs a majority vote.
Q. When would you use absolute_error instead of the default?

When the target contains outliers. Absolute error makes each leaf predict the
median, which is robust to a few extreme targets. The cost is a substantially
slower fit, since the median cannot be updated incrementally the way a mean can.
